title: Fire use by ancient humans just got a whole lot older
summary:
Imagine sitting around a campfire, roasting marshmallows. Now imagine doing that 1.8 million years ago. That's how far back a new discovery pushes the story of human fire use.

In South Africa's Wonderwerk Cave, scientists found burnt animal bones that hint our ancient relative Homo erectus used fire there as long as 1.8 million years ago. That's nearly twice as old as the previous record, which also came from this cave but dated to about 1 million years ago.

The new evidence comes from a deeper layer of sediment. Michael Chazan, an archaeologist at the University of Toronto who leads the excavations, is confident the fires were between 1.7 and 1.8 million years old.

The researchers used a clever technique called luminescence, which is normally used in forensics to solve crimes. When they shone blue light on the bones, the burnt ones glowed brighter than unburnt ones. The bones came from owl pellets—the balls of fur and bone that owls cough up after eating. Barn owls likely shared the cave with H. erectus, and the ancient humans kept fires going on the pellet-covered floor.

But don't picture H. erectus striking flint to start a fire. The earliest evidence of humans making sparks comes from only about 400,000 years ago. Instead, these early humans probably collected flames from wildfires and carried them into the cave. "This is not human ignition of fire. It's collecting a fire on the landscape," Chazan says.

The fires were likely for light and warmth, not cooking. And they weren't year-round—wildfires happen mainly in hot seasons, so fire access was limited. That might explain why H. erectus didn't make big lifestyle changes based on fire.

Still, this discovery pushes our understanding of when humans first tamed fire, even if they didn't create it. It's a fascinating glimpse into the lives of our ancient ancestors.
why_it_matters: For a 12–14-year-old, this discovery changes the story of human origins taught in school. It shows that fire—the force behind cooking, warmth, and later technology—was first borrowed from nature long before humans could create it.

background_read: Wonderwerk Cave is a deep cave in South Africa where archaeologists have found some of the oldest signs of early human life.
The cave's layers of sediment act like a time capsule, preserving bone and ash from more than a million years ago.
Homo erectus was an early human species, with bodies and walking patterns closer to modern humans than older ancestors, and it eventually spread from Africa into Asia and Europe.
Michael Chazan, an archaeologist at the University of Toronto (a leading Canadian research university), directs the excavations at Wonderwerk.
The new study pushes back the earliest known use of fire to around 1.8 million years ago, long before humans learned to start fires themselves.

perspectives.description: Archaeologists gain a much older reliable date for human fire use, confirming that early humans actively collected and kept fires. This matters because fire may have helped Homo erectus survive in caves and adapt to new environments.

The evidence is indirect — burnt bones in a pile of owl pellets, not a stone hearth — so some researchers may question how much we can really say about H. erectus behavior. The term 'fire use' can also be misleading if it means making fire, since these humans were collecting natural flames.

The finding fits a broader pattern: technologies often begin with opportunistic use before deliberate invention. H. erectus used fire when wildfires made it available, but did not yet reorganize life around it.

Further excavations at Wonderwerk and other ancient sites may reveal even older evidence, or show when humans learned to make fire themselves. If researchers can find traces of cooking or overnight occupation, the significance of these early campfires will become clearer.
